slides.title: Title
slides.notes: Open with the slogan that duality is not just another formula for the same object; it changes the operation being performed. The class should watch for two recurring moves: split a dual certificate into parts, and then ask whether a closure or qualification is needed to recover equality rather than only an inequality.

slides.title: Primal Dual Dictionary
slides.notes: Build the dictionary slowly. The left column describes operations on primal variables or primal epigraphs; the right column describes how the supporting slopes must be arranged after conjugacy. Emphasize that a dual formula is not a mnemonic table but a feasibility statement for affine lower bounds.

slides.title: Conjugate Of A Sum
slides.notes: Present the sum rule as a certificate splitting problem. To support f plus g with slope y, imagine assigning part of that slope to f and the remainder to g. The dual side minimizes over all such splits, and the closure term warns that the best split may only appear as a limit.

slides.title: Infimal Convolution
slides.notes: Now reverse the earlier point of view. Infimal convolution splits the primal point instead of the dual slope. It is the natural partner to addition because conjugacy swaps the role of choosing an x in a supremum with choosing compatible pieces whose sum or difference gives the displayed variable.

slides.title: Linear Image And Adjoint
slides.notes: Use this slide to connect dual operations with linear algebra students already know. The whole formula is forced by the pairing identity. A slope u on the target space becomes a slope A transpose u on the source space, and the infimum records all target slopes that pull back to the requested source slope.

slides.title: Support And Gauge Pairs
slides.notes: Keep the support and gauge cases connected to the previous formulas. They are not separate tricks; they are the same certificate translation applied to functions that encode sets. Support functions remember all linear inequalities of a set, while gauges remember how much scaling is needed to make a point feasible.

slides.title: Order Reversal
slides.notes: Treat order reversal as a quick error detector. If the primal function is raised, every affine payoff loses value, so the conjugate must go down. Many mistakes in dual operation algebra reveal themselves immediately because they preserve the inequality direction when conjugacy should have reversed it.

slides.title: Closure Qualifications
slides.notes: Pause here because closure terms are easy to rush past. The point is not that authors enjoy adding technical qualifiers. The closed epigraph is the object that conjugacy naturally sees. If a formal operation misses a boundary limit, a clean algebraic expression must be closed before it matches the dual object.

slides.title: Matrix Examples
slides.notes: Use quadratics as the clean computational laboratory. Every conjugate is explicit, the split problem is a small least squares calculation, and there is no domain boundary hiding the minimizer. This example helps students see why the infimal convolution formula is plausible before confronting singular or boundary-sensitive cases.

slides.title: Epigraph Transform View
slides.notes: Bring the class back to geometry rather than symbolic manipulation. Infimal convolution is produced by putting two epigraphs together, adding their costs, enforcing the split, and projecting away the auxiliary variable. Projection is exactly where closedness can be lost, so the closure term has a visible geometric source.

slides.title: Numerical Operation Checker
slides.notes: Connect the slide to the section notebook. The grid computation does not prove the theorem, but it makes the operation inspectable. Students should identify the chosen split, compare it with obvious feasible splits, and notice whether convexity residuals stay small or expose a failed hypothesis or too-small grid.

slides.title: Failure Modes
slides.notes: Use this as a diagnostic slide. Instead of saying that a theorem simply does not apply, ask which geometric component failed. Did the domains miss each other, did the minimizing split escape, did a projection lose a boundary point, or did the linear map send a dual variable into the wrong space?

slides.title: Rule Ledger
slides.notes: This ledger is the students' working reference. For each formula, have them say what is being split, what space the dual variable occupies, and what hypothesis controls closure. This habit prevents the common error of memorizing a dual operation while forgetting the feasibility problem that produced it.

slides.title: Learner Lab
slides.notes: Frame the lab as controlled experimentation. Students should not randomly edit every parameter at once. A useful run changes one domain, penalty, or matrix, then compares the visual consequence with the numerical residual. The goal is to identify which hypothesis is carrying the dual operation formula.

slides.title: Recap
slides.notes: Close by repeating the compact rule. Dual operations are certificate algebra: the primal operation determines how points or epigraphs are combined, conjugacy asks which slopes certify the result, and regularity decides whether the formal expression is already closed. This prepares the next material on constrained extremum problems.
